Who is credited with discovering Testosterone?
Testosterone: János Freud. Testosterone is the primary male sex hormone and androgen in males.
Who is credited with discovering Cyanoacrylate?
Cyanoacrylate: Harry Coover. The cyanoacrylate group in the monomer rapidly polymerizes in the presence of water to form long, strong chains.
Who is credited with discovering Rubidium?
Rubidium: Robert Bunsen. Rubidium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rb and atomic number 37.

Belonging to the birch family and numbering about 35 species, these monoecious trees and shrubs are found across the north temperate zone, with a few extending into Central America and the Andes — name this genus of tree?
Alder are trees of the genus Alnus in the birch family Betulaceae.
This unit of length equals one ten-billionth of a meter, or 100 picometres, and is named after a 19th-century Swedish physicist — what is it?
Angstrom (ONG-) is a unit of length equal to 1010 m; that is, one ten-billionth of a metre, a hundred-millionth of a centimetre, 0.1 nanometre, or 100 picometres.
This American physicist won a share of the 1927 Nobel Prize for an effect, now bearing his name, that demonstrated light's particle nature — who was he?
Arthur Compton (September 10, 1892 - March 15, 1962) was an American physicist who shared the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics with C. T. R. Wilson.
The first production aircraft of its type, this American military transport combines vertical takeoff and landing with long-range cruise performance—what is it?
Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey is an American multi-use, tiltrotor military transport and cargo aircraft with both vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) and short takeoff and landing (STOL) capabilities.
This leafy vegetable forms no head, just green blades atop pale bulbous stalks, with a flavor often compared to a mix of spinach and water chestnut — what vegetable is it?

Bok choy (American English, Canadian English, and Australian English), pak choi (British English, South African English, and Caribbean English) or pok choi is a type of Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp.
This soft, silvery-white metal shares group 12 of the periodic table with zinc and mercury, resembling zinc in its chemistry and mercury in its low melting point — what element, symbol Cd, is it?
Cadmium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cd and atomic number 48.
Named for the whisker-like barbels many species sport, these scaleless ray-finned fish include some of the largest freshwater giants in Southeast Asia and Eurasia — name this diverse group of fish?
Catfish are a diverse group of ray-finned fish of the order Siluriformes (historically Nematognathi).
A notorious household nuisance pest that feeds on sleeping humans, this insect has never been shown to actually transmit disease to people — what is it?
Cimex lectularius is a species of Cimicidae.
Entering service with Strategic Air Command in 1960, this four-engine, delta-wing supersonic bomber was the first in the world capable of Mach 2 — name the aircraft?

Convair B-58 Hustler is a supersonic strategic bomber, the first capable of Mach 2 flight. To achieve the high speeds desired, Convair chose a delta wing design used by contemporary interceptors such as the Convair F-102.
A staunch defender of Georg Cantor's set theory, this mathematician co-founded proof theory and became one of the most influential figures in his field — who is he?
David Hilbert (23 January 1862 - 14 February 1943) was a German mathematician and philosopher of mathematics and one of the most influential mathematicians of all time.
This waterfowl belongs to the same family as swans and geese, but is generally smaller and shorter-necked — and despite the shared family, swans and geese don't count as one. What is it?
Duck is the common name for numerous species of waterfowl in the family Anatidae.

It's the creation of economic value by spotting and commercializing opportunities — a venture that demands serious initiative and shoulders real risk. What is this process, named from a French word for the risk-taker who runs it?

Entrepreneurship is the creation or extraction of economic value by identifying and commercializing opportunities to deliver products or services, a process that typically requires considerable initiation and bears risk.
A legume plant from the family Fabaceae, its leaves and seeds have been common in dishes from the Indian subcontinent since ancient times — what is it?
Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) is an annual plant in the family Fabaceae, with leaves consisting of three small obovate to oblong leaflets.
Son of a wealthy Greek architect, this 2nd-century physician and philosopher's writings shaped anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and neurology for centuries after his death — who is he?
This applied art and academic discipline uses text and images to craft visual communications aimed at specific audiences and objectives — what field is it?
Graphic design is a profession, academic discipline and applied art that involves creating visual communications intended to transmit specific messages to social groups, with specific objectives.
Credited with putting middle-class Americans behind the wheel, this industrialist lent his surname to the very philosophy of assembly-line manufacturing. Who is he?
Henry Ford (July 30, 1863 - April 7, 1947) was an American industrialist and business magnate.
This endocrine condition floods the body with thyroid hormone, causing a racing heart, heat intolerance, tremor, and weight loss — and a rare 'storm' can be deadly; what is it?
Hyperthyroidism is a endocrine disease in which the thyroid gland produces excessive amounts of thyroid hormones.

A colorless, flammable organic compound with a pungent odor, this liquid is miscible in water, ethanol, and chloroform, and is widely used as a solvent and disinfectant. It's commonly abbreviated as IPA—what is it?
Isopropyl alcohol (IUPAC name propan-2-ol and also called isopropanol or 2-propanol, commonly abbreviated as IPA) is a colorless, flammable, organic compound with a pungent odor.

An Alberta-raised classical liberal who earned his PhD in clinical psychology at McGill and taught at Harvard before the University of Toronto, this commentator drew huge attention in the late 2010s — who is he?
Jordan Peterson (born 12 June 1962) is a Canadian psychologist, author, and media commentator.
This American economist served as U.S. Treasury Secretary, later led the National Economic Council, and was the 27th president of Harvard before resigning a professorship there in 2026 — who is he?
Larry Summers (born November 30, 1954) is an American economist.
Known mainly from fossils in Peru's Pisco Formation, this Miocene-era macroraptorial sperm whale takes its name from a biblical sea monster — what is it called?
Livyatan is an extinct genus of highly predatory macroraptorial sperm whale, containing one known species: L. melvillei.
Its Spanish name translates to 'little apple of death' — this tropical tree's apple-like fruit and toxic milky sap make it one of the most poisonous trees on Earth — which tree?
Manchineel (Hippomane mancinella), also known as the tree of death, is a species of flowering plant in the spurge family (Euphorbiaceae).

Patented in 1922 and used to relieve pain, fever, and spasms, this drug's sale is restricted in some countries due to a rare but serious blood-cell side effect discovered in the 1970s — what drug is it?
Metamizole is a painkiller, spasm reliever, and fever reliever drug.
First synthesized in 2003 by Russian and American scientists at Dubna, this synthetic element — atomic number 115 — was named in 2016 for the oblast around its birthplace — what is it?
Moscovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mc and atomic number 115.
Found in tiny native amounts in Earth's crust but riding inside iron meteorites that never met oxygen, this hard, ductile metal shares its name with a small coin — which element is it?
Nickel is a chemical element; it has symbol Ni and atomic number 28.
These red-haired great apes once roamed all of Southeast Asia but now cling to just Borneo and Sumatra — and in 2017 scientists confirmed a brand-new third species among them. Which animal is it?
Orangutan are great apes native to the rainforests of Indonesia and Malaysia.
Which American biologist became famous for the controversial 1968 book 'The Population Bomb' and its dire warnings about population growth, famine, and resource depletion?

Paul R. Ehrlich (May 29, 1932 - March 13, 2026) was an American biologist, author, and environmentalist known for his predictions and warnings about the consequences of population growth, including famine and resource depletion.

This class of lipid molecules has a water-loving 'head' built around a phosphate group and two water-fearing fatty-acid 'tails' — and forms an essential building block of neuronal membranes in the brain. Name the class of molecule?

Phospholipid are a class of lipids whose molecule has a hydrophilic "head" containing a phosphate group and two hydrophobic "tails" derived from fatty acids, joined by an alcohol residue (usually a glycerol molecule).
Known as little hogweed or pursley, every part of this succulent plant can be eaten raw or cooked — what plant is it?
Portulaca oleracea (common purslane, also known as little hogweed, or pursley) is a succulent plant in the family Portulacaceae.
This set of three positive whole numbers, like (3, 4, 5), satisfies a squared plus b squared equals c squared and forms the side lengths of a right triangle — what is it called?
Pythagorean triple consists of three positive integers a, b, and c, such that a2 + b2 = c2.
As chairman of the now-defunct Purdue Pharma, he oversaw the launch of OxyContin — a tenure dramatized in Hulu's Dopesick and Netflix's Painkiller; who is he?
Richard Sackler (born March 10, 1945) is an American businessman, pharmaceutical entrepreneur and physician who was the chairman and president of Purdue Pharma, a now-defunct pharmaceutical company.

Often striking suddenly after heavy lifting and described as a shooting pain down one leg, about 90% of cases trace to a spinal disc herniation pressing on a nerve root — what's this condition called?
Sciatica is pain going down the leg from the lower back.
This Irish mathematician and physicist held Cambridge's Lucasian chair for a record 54 years and lent his name to a theorem in vector calculus and to equations of fluid motion — who was he?
Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet (stohks; 13 August 1819 - 1 February 1903), was an Irish mathematician and physicist.
This round, gram-positive germ lives harmlessly on most people's skin and noses, but turn opportunistic and it triggers abscesses, sinus infections, and food poisoning. What is it?

Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive spherically shaped bacterium, a member of the Bacillota, and is a usual member of the microbiota of the body, frequently found in the upper respiratory tract and on the skin.
These large, often hairy spiders of the family Theraphosidae number over a thousand species, and New World pet varieties can flick irritating 'urticating hairs' at threats. What creatures are they?
Tarantula are a group of large and often hairy spiders of the family Theraphosidae.

Affecting roughly 10 to 15 percent of people, this condition causes a person to hear ringing or other sounds with no external source, and its name comes from the Latin word for 'to ring' — what is it?
Tinnitus is a condition when a person hears a ringing sound or a different variety of sounds when no corresponding external sound is present and that other people cannot hear.
This medical specialty, whose name derives from the Greek word for urine, covers surgical and medical treatment of the urinary tract and the male reproductive organs — name this field?

Urology (from Greek ouron "urine" and - -logia "study of"), also known as genitourinary surgery, is the branch of medicine that focuses on surgical and medical diseases of the urinary system and the male reproductive organs.
The first-ever recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics, this German scientist discovered a form of electromagnetic radiation named after him in some languages — who was he?

Wilhelm Röntgen (27 March 1845 - 10 February 1923) was a German experimental physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays (known as Rntgen rays in many languages).

This symptom can stem from something as mild as gastroenteritis or as serious as a ruptured aortic aneurysm or ectopic pregnancy, yet its exact cause goes unexplained in about a third of cases — what symptom is this?
Native to China and Taiwan, this fast-growing deciduous tree can reach 15 meters in 25 years and has become notorious in North America as a host plant for the invasive spotted lanternfly. What is it?
Ailanthus altissima: Deciduous tree in the quassia family.
This military pilot became his country's first astronaut when he flew to the International Space Station aboard a 2024 mission — who is he?
Alper Gezeravcı: Turkish fighter pilot and astronaut (born 1979)

Coming on slowly it brings vague fatigue and breathlessness; arriving suddenly it can cause confusion and fainting — and only when it's severe does a person look pale — which blood disorder reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying ability?
Anemia: Reduced ability of blood to carry oxygen.
This genus of orb-weaving spiders, encompassing the European garden spider and the barn spider among its 500-plus species, was named by an 18th-century Swedish naturalist in 1757 — which genus?
Araneus: Genus of spiders. The genus was erected by Carl Alexander Clerck in 1757.

Related to the tufted and horned members of its family found in the Pacific, this seabird breeds from Iceland to Newfoundland and dives underwater to catch zooplankton, small fish and crabs — which auk is this?
Atlantic puffin: Species of seabird. The Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica), also known as the common puffin, is a species of seabird in the auk family.
Bred in Britain to hunt rabbits and hares, this scent hound's keen nose also makes it a popular detection dog for smuggled food at airports — which breed?
Beagle: Breed of small scent hound. The Beagle is a British breed of scent hound, similar in appearance to the much larger foxhound.
Patented in 1976 and sold under the brand name Zebeta, this beta-1-selective medication treats high blood pressure and heart failure — what is it?
Bisoprolol: Beta-1 selective adrenenergic blocker medication used to treat cardiovascular diseases.
Hailing from the Anglo-Scottish frontier and frequently cited as the most intelligent dog breed on Earth, which sheepdog dominates sheepdog trials?
Border Collie: Working dog breed. The Border Collie is a breed of British herding dog of the collie type of medium size.
Encompassing reporting, dashboards, data mining, and analytics, this set of strategies and technologies helps companies turn raw data into strategic decisions — what's it called?
Business intelligence: Strategies for analysis and use of data.
Nicknamed for its heart-shaped seed pods, this mustard-family weed is considered protocarnivorous because its seeds ooze a mucilage that traps nematodes — which species?
Capsella bursa-pastoris: Species of flowering plant in the mustard family.

This biological process splits a parent into two daughters, either producing genetically identical copies via mitosis or reducing chromosome number by half via meiosis to form gametes. What process is it?
Cell division: Biological process. Cell division usually occurs as part of a larger cell cycle in which the cell grows and replicates its chromosome(s) before dividing.

This antibiotic is used as an eye ointment for conjunctivitis and, when safer options fail, to treat meningitis, plague, cholera, and typhoid — but in newborns it can trigger a dangerous swelling condition called gray baby syndrome — what drug is it?
Chloramphenicol: Antibiotic. Chloramphenicol is an antibiotic useful for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
This French inventor born near Toulouse is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer, but in 1870 he was also among the first to take up the sport of cycling in France — who is it?
Clément Ader: French inventor and engineer (1841–1925)

Native to Europe and North Africa, this member of the carrot family can grow to 8 feet tall, with hollow stems blotched dark maroon and a distinctly foul smell carried on the wind — which highly poisonous plant is this?
Conium maculatum: Poisonous plant. The plant is herbaceous, with no woody parts, and has a biennial lifecycle.
A creeping vine of the gourd family that originated across India, Nepal, and southern China, this plant comes in slicing, pickling, and seedless types — what is it?
Cucumber: Species of flowering plant with edible fruits.

This acute medical syndrome develops over hours or days and causes disturbed attention, awareness, and sometimes hallucinations — often triggered by illness, substances, or their withdrawal — what is it called?
Delirium: Severe confusion that develops quickly, and often fluctuates in intensity.
A dentist and gambler who fought alongside lawman Wyatt Earp at the O.K. Corral, his reputation claimed dozens of killings though researchers count just one to three — who was this gunfighter?
Doc Holliday: Gambler, gunfighter, and dentist in the American West (1851–1887)
After stints at the CIA, Dell, and Booz Allen Hamilton, this NSA contractor flew to Hong Kong in 2013 and leaked thousands of classified documents exposing global surveillance — who is he?
Edward Snowden: Whistleblower and NSA contractor (born 1983)
One of the four basic animal tissue types, this thin protective cell layer lines blood vessels and body cavities and includes the skin's outer layer — what is it called?
Epithelium: Tissue lining the surfaces of organs in animals.
In this small bird of prey, females can be up to 25% larger than males — one of the biggest size gaps between sexes of any bird — and it hunts garden songbirds across Europe and Asia — which raptor?

Eurasian sparrowhawk: Species of bird. The Eurasian sparrowhawk (Accipiter nisus), also known as the northern sparrowhawk or simply the sparrowhawk, is a small bird of prey in the family Accipitridae.
Marketed under brand names like Allegra, this second-generation antihistamine treats allergy symptoms without crossing the blood-brain barrier the way older drugs do — what medication is it?
Fexofenadine: Antihistamine medication. Fexofenadine is an antihistamine medication used in the treatment of allergy symptoms such as allergic rhinitis and urticaria.
Dead at just 26, this British thinker had already reshaped philosophy, mathematics and economics — and as an undergraduate translated Wittgenstein's 'Tractatus' into English; who was he?
Frank P. Ramsey: British philosopher, mathematician and economist (1903–1930)
With a siphon that can stretch over three feet and a shell just 6 to 8 inches across, this giant Pacific burrowing clam can live up to 179 years — which creature?
Caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and colloquially called 'the clap,' this sexually transmitted infection can pass from mother to child during birth — what is it?
Gonorrhea: Sexually transmitted infection. Gonorrhea or gonorrhoea, colloquially known as the clap, is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Caused by a retrovirus that attacks the immune system, this condition has no cure or vaccine — yet with antiretroviral treatment a person can now expect to live a normal life and die with the virus, not of it. What is it?
HIV/AIDS: Spectrum of conditions caused by HIV infection.
The only Saskatchewan-born Nobel laureate, this Canadian-born chemist won the 1983 prize for unraveling the mechanisms of electron-transfer reactions in metal complexes — who was he?

Galaxies recede from Earth at speeds proportional to their distance, a relationship credited to a 1929 paper — though the maths behind an expanding universe had already been derived in 1922 by Alexander Friedmann. What's this relationship called?
Hubble's law: Observation in physical cosmology.
This 14th-century Arab scholar wrote his most famous work, the Muqaddimah, in just six months and once met the conqueror Tamerlane — who is he?
Ibn Khaldun: Arab Islamic scholar, historian and philosopher (1332–1406)
This 12th-century polymath from Mesopotamia wrote a treatise describing 50 ingenious mechanical devices, including his famous elephant clock, earning him the title 'father of robotics' — who is he?
Ismail al-Jazari: Muslim engineer and artist (1136–1206)
Once an assistant to astronomer Tycho Brahe and later imperial mathematician to Emperor Rudolf II, this polymath formulated the laws of planetary motion — who was he?
Johannes Kepler: German astronomer and mathematician (1571–1630)
Named from a Tongan and Marquesan word meaning 'bitter,' this pepper-family plant's ground root becomes a ceremonial Pacific Islands drink that numbs the mouth — what is it?
Kava: Species of plant. Kava or kava kava (Piper methysticum: Latin 'pepper' and Latinized Greek 'intoxicating') is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands.
A genus of 47 flowering plant species in the sage family, prized for its fragrant oil and used in traditional medicine, cosmetics, and as a culinary herb across Mediterranean climates — which genus?
Lavandula: Genus of plants. Lavandula (common name lavender) is a genus of 47 known species of perennial flowering plants in the sage family, Lamiaceae.
Soft, movable, and painless, this benign fatty-tissue growth most often shows up under the skin on the upper back, shoulders, or abdomen — what is it?
Lipoma: Benign tumor made of fat tissue.
This common, nonspecific medical sign involves lymph nodes becoming abnormally swollen or enlarged, with causes ranging from the common cold to cancer. What's the condition called?
Lymphadenopathy: Abnormal change in size of the lymph nodes.
This American cultural anthropologist's 1928 fieldwork, Coming of Age in Samoa, made her a household name for exploring adolescence and sexuality in Pacific societies — who is she?
Nicknamed a 'semi-lunar' cartilage for its half-moon shape, this crescent-shaped structure cushions joints like the knee, wrist, and jaw — what is it?
Meniscus (anatomy): Fibrocartilaginous part of a bone joint.
Known to NATO as 'Flogger,' this Soviet variable-sweep-wing fighter was the first in the country's air force to carry look-down/shoot-down radar, with over 5,000 built. Which aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23: Soviet fighter-interceptor aircraft introduced in 1970.
Native to northern India, this fast-growing, drought-resistant tree is nicknamed the 'drumstick tree' for its seed pods and the 'horseradish tree' for its pungent roots — what is it?
Moringa oleifera: Species of flowering tree.
Originating near the Beijing region and used throughout East Asian cooking, this Brassica rapa vegetable spread to Europe, the Americas, and Australia during the 20th century — which vegetable is it?
Napa cabbage: Subspecies of flowering plant.
Humphry Davy coined this colorless gas's cheerful nickname for the euphoria it brings, and it still earns a spot on the WHO's Essential Medicines list for dentistry and surgery. What is it?
Nitrous oxide: Colourless non-flammable greenhouse gas.
This biological process turns a primary oocyte into an egg cell capable of developing once fertilized, beginning during embryonic development — what is it called?
Oogenesis: Egg cell production process. Oogenesis or ovogenesis is the differentiation of the ovum (egg cell) into a cell competent to further develop when fertilized.
Sold under the brand name Protonix, this proton-pump inhibitor treats ulcers and acid reflux but can, with long-term use, cause vitamin B12 deficiency and low magnesium — what is this drug?
This term describes a short chain of amino acids joined by a particular kind of bond; string together enough of them (10,000 daltons or more) and you get a protein instead — what is it?
Peptide: Short chains of 2–50 amino acids.

For two thousand years it lived inside natural philosophy alongside chemistry and biology, only breaking off as its own discipline during the 17th-century Scientific Revolution; what is this study of matter, energy, and force?
Physics: Scientific field of study. It is one of the most fundamental scientific disciplines.
Built from many linked simple sugars and including starch, glycogen, and cellulose among its examples, this class of carbohydrate is the most abundant in our food — what is it called?
Polysaccharide: Long carbohydrate polymers such as starch, glycogen, cellulose, and chitin.
Known by folk names like 'bird cherry' and 'Mayday tree,' this flowering plant in the rose family is native to Europe and northern Asia — what species is it?
Prunus padus: Species of flowering plant in the rose family.
The largest of the procyonid family, this North American mammal is famous for its facial mask, ringed tail, and remarkably dexterous front paws — which animal is it?
Raccoon: Medium-sized mammal native to North America.
Discovered in 1803 by William Hyde Wollaston and named for the rose color of one of its compounds, this rare silvery-white metal of the platinum group is used to enhance jewelry — which element?
Rhodium: Chemical element with atomic number 45 (Rh)
Extremely cold-hardy and thriving in poor soil, this cereal grass is a staple grain behind Scandinavian crispbread and a certain whiskey style — what is it?
Rye: Species of grain. Rye (Secale cereale) is a grass grown extensively as a grain, a cover crop and a forage crop.
Nicknamed 'Devil's Breath' and derived from nightshade plants, which motion-sickness drug has also been used historically as a deliriant?
Resembling a long-nosed mouse but actually a closer relative of hedgehogs and moles, this small mammal has sharp spike-like teeth rather than gnawing incisors — what is it?
Mostly made from potato starch but also found in apples and berries, this slowly-metabolized sugar alcohol is an isomer of mannitol, differing only at one hydroxyl group. What is it?
Common in coastal tropical waters worldwide, this group of cartilaginous fish includes about 220 species across 29 genera, from butterfly rays to manta and devil rays — what are they?
Its explosive yield became the standard yardstick for comparing bombs and even asteroid impacts; chemists also use it to make charge-transfer salts — what's this nitro compound?

This geometry rule holds that a triangle inscribed in a circle, with one side running through the center as a diameter, always has a right angle at its third point — proved by Euclid, though occasionally miscredited to Pythagoras. What's it called?
Thales's theorem: On triangles inscribed in a circle with a diameter as an edge.
Called the "Father of Japanese Botany," this grammar-school dropout collected over 500,000 plant specimens and earned a doctorate — and his birthday is now Botany Day in Japan. Who was he?
Also known as 45,X, which chromosomal condition affects only females who are born with a single X chromosome instead of two, often causing short stature and a webbed neck?
Turner syndrome: X chromosome monosomy. Small chin (micrognathia), loose folds of skin on the neck, slanted eyelids and prominent ears are found in Turner syndrome, though not all will show it.
Also called vervain, this genus of roughly 150 flowering plant species is native mostly to the Americas and Asia, though its European type species grows wild there too — what genus is it?
Verbena: Genus of plants. Verbena, also known as vervain or (in obsolete spelling) verveine, is a genus in the family Verbenaceae.

With black-tipped wings and long red legs and bill, this long-distance migrant famously avoids the open Mediterranean, detouring instead via Gibraltar or the Levant on its way to African wintering grounds — which bird is it?
White stork: Species of bird. The white stork (Ciconia ciconia) is a large bird in the stork family, Ciconiidae.
Marketed under the brand name Imovane, this 'Z-drug' sedative treats insomnia by boosting GABA activity in the brain much like a benzodiazepine, though it's chemically distinct — what is it?
The symbol for phosphorus is P. Phosphorus is a chemical element; it has symbol P and atomic number 15.

In what year was Nicole Scherzinger born?

In what year was Seth MacFarlane born?
Seth MacFarlane: Seth Woodbury MacFarlane (born October 26, 1973) is an American actor, animator, writer, producer, director, comedian, and singer.

Stellan Skarsgård: Stellan John Skarsgård (Swedish: [ˈstɛ̂lːan ˈskɑ̌ːʂɡoːɖ]; born 13 June 1951) is a Swedish actor.
In what year was Helen McCrory born?
Helen McCrory: Helen Elizabeth McCrory (17 August 1968 – 16 April 2021) was an English actress.

Joe Rogan: Joseph James Rogan Jr. (born August 11, 1967) is an American podcaster, UFC color commentator, comedian, actor, and former television host.

Gabriel Macht: Gabriel Swann Macht (born January 22, 1972) is an American actor, known for his role as Harvey Specter in the USA Network series Suits (2011–2019).
In what year was Jim Carrey born?
Jim Carrey: James Eugene Carrey (born January 17, 1962) is a Canadian and American actor and comedian.
In what year was Alia Bhatt born?
Alia Bhatt (born 15 March 1993) is a British actress of Indian descent who predominantly works in Hindi films.
In what year was Kevin Hart born?
Kevin Hart: Kevin Darnell Hart (born July 6, 1979) is an American comedian and actor.
In what year was Ronald Reagan born?
Ronald Reagan: Ronald Wilson Reagan (February 6, 1911 – June 5, 2004) was an American politician and actor who served as the 40th president of the United States from 1981 to 1989.
In what year did Lance Reddick die?
Lance Reddick: Lance Solomon Reddick (June 7, 1962 – March 17, 2023) was an American actor.
In what year was Pulp Fiction first released?
Pulp Fiction is a 1994 American crime film written and directed by Quentin Tarantino from a story he conceived with Roger Avary.
In what year was Tár first released?
Tár is a 2022 psychological drama film written and directed by Todd Field.
In what year was Finestkind first released?
Finestkind is a 2023 American crime thriller film written and directed by Brian Helgeland.
In what year was May December first released?
May December: It stars Natalie Portman as an actress who travels to meet and study the life of Gracie (Julianne Moore), a sex offender she is set to play in a film.
